Units of work

A unit of work is a body of work that several goals share one branch for: a feature, a shared bug, a refactor, a contract change. Goals that declare a unit are built on that unit's branch instead of the main one.

Nothing changes unless you opt in

A goal that declares no unit runs exactly as it always did, cut from the configured base branch. Units are for repositories where more than one goal belongs to the same piece of work.

The branch shape

Three kinds of branch, each cut by someone different.

main                              the integration branch
 +-- feature/<name>               the unit: goals share it
      +-- sdlc/<goal>             one per goal, cut from the unit branch
      +-- feature/<name>/<sub>    a dependency found mid-flight
BranchWhat it isWho cuts it
feature/<name>The unit. Several people share it.A person, before the first goal.
sdlc/<goal>One goal, cut fresh from its base each time.Sigma, when the goal is picked.
feature/<name>/<sub>Work found mid-flight under a unit.A person.
Nobody commits directly to a unit branch

Every change reaches feature/<name> as a pull request from a goal branch. Sigma can detect some direct commits before it force-pushes a unit branch; it cannot prevent one. Only your host's branch protection can prevent it.

How an issue declares its unit

An issue declares its unit twice, on purpose: a feature:<name> label for machines to query, and a bare Feature: <name> line in the body for people to read. If they disagree, the body wins. Several natural-looking ways of writing the body line declare nothing, silently, so copy the shape from the branching contract linked below.

  • A unit name cannot contain / and must be something git accepts as a branch segment.
  • The prefix stays feature/ even for a shared bug, so every unit branch is searchable.

Opening a unit

/sigma-define opens the branch, the label and the registry entry, and files the issues that declare the unit. The order of those parts matters; the command does them in the order that works. You are also asked one optional question: does this unit get a priority (P0 to P4)? Skip it and nothing changes.

What happens when a goal is picked

  1. The base is chosen

    A declared unit means the goal is cut from that unit's branch. No declaration means the configured base. A declared unit whose branch does not exist stops the start, loudly.

  2. The registry is brought up to date

    The unit's entry records which goals belong to it, so a deleted branch does not take that knowledge with it.

  3. Upkeep may run

    If rebase upkeep is on, the unit's branch is brought forward before the goal is cut.

  4. The worktree is cut

    Work happens on the goal's own branch. Anything Sigma files from the goal, such as a follow-up, is stamped with the same unit.

If the issue names a unit whose feature: label does not exist, the pick is set aside with sdlc:needs-label and resumes by itself once a person creates the label. That check runs on any repository, adopted or not.

The registry

A repository adopts units by having a committed .sdlc/features/ folder. It holds one record per unit (title, owner, repositories, goals in pick order, and an optional priority) and a human-readable page per unit with a block Sigma regenerates and a region that is yours. The index is derived, never edited. Without the folder, the registry-backed steps do nothing.

Pick order

Among goals that can be picked, order is decided by four things in turn.

Pick order among eligible goals. A P0 issue in any unit still beats every P1, whatever either unit's priority is.

Unit priority is on by default and has no effect until a unit has a recorded priority. Turn it off by setting discovery.feature_priority.enabled to false. One limit: when the label queue is the source, the reorder sees only the 200 oldest matching issues, so on a deeper backlog a newly filed P0 can wait. Reading the board directly as the queue avoids that.

Landing a unit

Merging a goal into the unit branch is not the merge that ships the work. Getting feature/<name> onto the main branch is a separate step, by default a person's. Sigma closes the goal's issue itself after the merge; a Closes #N line does not do it. A stale unit branch is caught up with /sigma-rebase.

Keeping unit branches current: upkeep and rebase

A unit branch lives for as long as its work does, and its base keeps moving. If nobody brings the unit forward, the gap grows and the final merge becomes one large conflict. Upkeep replays a unit branch onto the current base, pushes the result with a lease, and keeps the tip it replaced as a backup. It is opt-in, and with it off nothing on this page happens.

What upkeep does and does not do

  • It replays an existing unit branch onto its base and pushes with a lease. Every push is a force-push on the exact tip it read, so if the remote moved meanwhile the push is refused and tried again on the next pass.
  • It never deletes a unit branch. The only deletion it makes is pruning old backups.
  • It never commits to a unit branch itself; it only replays commits that already exist.
  • It does not land a unit. Landing is a separate, guarded step that a person asks for.
  • It does not run a language model to resolve a conflict unless you set the conflict level to agent. With no spend key set, that level has no spend limit.

Two ways a unit is brought forward

WayWhen it runsControlled by
At pick timeWhen a goal that declares a unit is picked, the unit branch and the goal’s branch are brought up to date first. If another pass holds the unit’s rebase lock, the pick does not wait; it cuts the goal, re-checks the unit tip right after, and moves the still-empty goal branch if the tip changed.work.rebase_upkeep, on by default; off turns it off.
On a windowOne bounded sweep brings every unit that is behind its base up to date, at most once per window.The three opt-ins below.

Both use the same per-unit engine, so backups, the lease, the direct-commit refusal and conflict handling behave the same in either.

Turning the schedule on

All three of these must be present. Any other spelling of a value (the text “true”, the number 1) leaves it closed.

  1. upkeep.enabled

    Set it to the JSON boolean true in .sdlc/config.json. The scaffold writes the block with it off; a repository adopted earlier copies the block in from the template.

  2. ledger.enabled

    Set it to exactly true. The watcher that runs the schedule is the ledger watcher. Remove a leftover stop file for the watcher first, or it exits at once.

  3. SIGMA_UPKEEP_JOB=1

    Set this environment variable to exactly 1 in the environment of the process that starts the sweep, on one machine. Two opted-in machines would both start passes; the lease makes the second push refuse, but each wastes a fetch and a replay. To split units between machines on purpose, use upkeep.units.include and upkeep.units.exclude.

Then set work.base to your default branch. With it empty, every pass ends with no base and does nothing; the doctor says so. Upkeep also refuses a unit branch as the base unless you name it in work.integration_base. Before relying on it, look at what it would do and run one pass by hand on a unit you can afford to rewrite. The commands, which you type:

python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py preview .sdlc
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py show .sdlc <unit>
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py upkeep .sdlc <unit>

preview lists every unit the sweep would take with a predicted outcome and moves nothing (a predicted conflict is a probe, and a real rebase may differ). show reports on one unit and moves nothing. upkeep runs one pass.

The window

The schedule does not poll each unit. It works on a window, upkeep.window_hours (default 12).

  • When it opens. When this machine has no completed sweep on record, or window_hours have passed since the last completed one ended.
  • Who starts the sweep, whichever comes first once it opens: the first session start on the machine (which starts a detached sweep and returns at once), the ledger watcher’s next tick, or a merge made through Sigma on the machine that merged.
  • What a closed window costs. One small file read and some arithmetic. No git call, no GitHub call.
  • What a sweep does. It takes a job lock, lists the units the include and exclude lists admit (exclude always wins), and runs the per-unit pass for each, one at a time. A unit already at its base costs one bounded read. The units come from the registry alone; a remote unit branch with no registry record is not maintained, and the doctor names it.
  • Failures do not spread. A unit that is refused, parked or failed does not stop the others. One sweep at a time: another sweep holding the lock makes the new one back off, which is a refusal, not a failure.
  • The time cap. All units share one wall-clock cap: upkeep.verify.timeout_minutes (default 60) plus a fixed 15-minute margin. A unit the cap prevented from starting is listed as unreached and waits for the next window.
  • Where it runs. Detached, with only an allowlisted environment. Windows is refused, and the status file says so once.
StampWritten whenEffect
CompletedA sweep ran to the end, even if some units were refused, parked or unreached.Closes the window for window_hours.
AttemptedA sweep started, or was cut short before useful work: killed, found busy, failed to spawn, or every unit failed.Holds off a re-trigger for upkeep.retry_minutes (default 60) only; never closes the window.

So a sweep that dies does not cost you a day: the next session start or watcher tick after the retry time starts it again. A missing or unreadable stamp reads as an open window, and a completed time dated in the future counts as no completed sweep, so a clock set far ahead cannot silence upkeep.

Backups and the lease

Each time a pass rewrites a unit branch it keeps the old tip as a backup ref under a Sigma namespace, in the same atomic push as the update, so both land or neither does. A pure fast-forward replaces nothing and writes no backup. Two commands manage them, and both do nothing while upkeep is off:

python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py restore .sdlc <unit> --list
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py restore .sdlc <unit> <stamp> --expect <tip>
python3 <installed-sigma>/skills/sigma-loop/scripts/feature_rebase.py prune .sdlc --dry-run
  • Restore puts the branch back at a named backup. You state the tip the branch has now, and the push is leased on it: if the branch moved, nothing changes. The tip being replaced is kept as a new backup. A restore is not sticky; the next pick or sweep brings the branch forward again, so set work.rebase_upkeep to off first if you want it to stay.
  • Prune removes backups older than upkeep.backup.keep_days (default 14) while always keeping the newest upkeep.backup.keep_last (default 5) of each unit. The sweep prunes by itself once per sweep.

Nobody commits directly to a unit branch

Every change reaches feature/<name> as a pull request from a goal branch. Before it force-pushes, a pass asks of every commit on the branch whether a pull request accounts for it. If one is not accounted for, the pass refuses with direct-commits, leaves the branch exactly as it was, and files the finding as tracked work. A later pass that finds none closes the finding.

If a commit did arrive through a pull request but its subject carries no trace of it, you acknowledge it with the ack verb of the same script (ack .sdlc <unit> <sha>, or --all for the commits the filed issue listed). The acknowledgement survives the rewrite it unblocks and travels by pull request to every teammate.

Sigma detects; only your host can prevent

Sigma notices some direct commits before it force-pushes; it cannot stop one. Only host branch protection can. Ordinary protection on unit branches blocks upkeep’s own force-push, so grant upkeep’s account a bypass.

Conflicts

upkeep.conflicts.resolveWhat happens to a conflicted unit
off (default)The unit branch is left untouched, nothing is pushed, and one issue records why.
mechanicalA conflict confined to the changelog is resolved by a heading-aware union, proved, and pushed once. Anything else is parked. Needs a verify command unless mechanical_without_verify is true.
agentA capped headless resolver plus an independent reviewer. Set max_budget_usd_per_unit, and optionally a daily ceiling, to cap it.

A parked conflict is one finding. Before filing, the pass looks for an open issue with the same conflict id and comments on it at most once a day. A replay that would delete content the branch has is a blocked pass, not a clean one.

When a person uses /sigma-rebase

/sigma-rebase is the attended counterpart of upkeep. Upkeep runs on its own, once per pick or window, and stops cold at a conflict. /sigma-rebase runs whenever you ask, explains itself, and walks you through a real conflict instead of leaving a bare git error. Reach for it when:

  • a unit branch is stale and you want it current now, without waiting for a window;
  • upkeep parked a conflict and you want to resolve it with context;
  • you want to see what the base changed before you move anything.

It always shows a brief first: what each commit the base picked up says, in its changelog entry, pull request or design write-up, or an honest note that no written reason exists, plus the files both sides touched, so conflicts are named before the rebase runs. Then it asks you to confirm. On confirmation it rebases only the branch you are on, never one you are not sitting in, autostashes a dirty tree, and pushes with a lease.

On a conflict it shows, per file, the base-side commits that touched it (or the one that deleted it, and why) and offers named options: keep this branch’s version, follow a move if the code went elsewhere, accept the base’s decision, or resolve by hand. It refuses to continue if a resolution would silently drop a commit as empty, and you can abort at any point to leave the tree as it was. Once clean it runs your verify command and only then asks whether to merge; answering no leaves everything rebased but unmerged. Anyone may run it on any branch; it has no authorisation layer.

When something goes wrong

What happenedRecovery
The sweep was killed or the machine rebootedAutomatic: re-triggered after the retry time.
The sweep hit its time capAutomatic: unreached units wait for the next window.
The remote moved during a pushAutomatic: the next pass tries again.
Direct commits on the branchReview, then acknowledge, or move the work onto a goal branch.
A conflictResolve it with /sigma-rebase, or set the conflict level to mechanical for changelog conflicts.
A bad rewriteRestore from the backup.
A job hangsCreate the upkeep stop file in .sdlc/state/; Sigma never deletes it for you.

To stop upkeep entirely, set upkeep.enabled to false. Landing a whole unit onto its base is a separate, guarded gesture that is never automatic; it rehearses by default and merges only the exact head it verified.

Not measured: upkeep has been run end to end on a local remote and on one private throwaway repository. It has not been measured at tens of units, against branch rulesets with bypass actors, or with a real model resolving conflicts. One sweep per window per machine means at most two a day at the default. The keys are on All settings.

Technical detail

The rules, defaults and guarantees are in the branching contract; a guided walk from issue to merge is in how branching works. Where the two differ, the contract is right.
